title: The City of Joy
author: Dominique Lapierre
target_audience: General adult readers interested in India and social issues
Readers drawn to human rights, poverty, and inspirational stories
Students of history, cultural studies, and social work
Anyone seeking real-life accounts of resilience and compassion
core_themes: Human resilience in the face of poverty
Hope and dignity among the disenfranchised
Impact of social inequality and systemic oppression
primary_purpose: To illuminate the lives, struggles, and unwavering spirit of the poorest residents of a Kolkata slum (Anand Nagar, or 'the City of Joy'), highlighting their humanity, hope, and capacity for joy amid extremes of hardship.

structure_format.narrative_style: Immersive, narrative nonfiction blending journalistic observation with novelistic storytelling
structure_format.organization: Chronological and character-driven, following key individuals' intertwined stories

key_concepts_lessons: Dignity and happiness can flourish even in dire circumstances.
The power of selflessness, faith, and mutual aid transforms communities.
Learning from the marginalized can inspire personal growth and reevaluation of privilege.
Complex interweaving of religion, culture, and poverty shapes the lives of the urban poor.
Individual stories can humanize and elevate understanding of broader social issues.
notable_features: Based on immersive, on-location research among Kolkata’s poorest citizens
Profiles real figures including Polish priest Father Stephan Kovalski (inspired by real-life Father Gaston Dayanand)
Mixes sociological reporting with intimate storytelling
Led to international awareness and philanthropy focused on India’s slum dwellers
cultural_historical_context: Written during the 1980s, following Lapierre’s extended stays in Kolkata, 'The City of Joy' highlighted widespread poverty and social stratification during a period of rapid urbanization in India, drawing Western attention to issues rarely depicted with such nuance.
reception_impact: International bestseller, translated into over 30 languages
Praised for its compassion, insight, and storytelling
Inspired a major motion picture (1992, starring Patrick Swayze)
Galvanized charitable work and NGO involvement in Kolkata
Some critics noted the risks of an outsider’s perspective and potential for sentimentalism
comparable_titles: Behind the Beautiful Forevers by Katherine Boo
Shantaram by Gregory David Roberts (though partly fiction)
Half the Sky by Nicholas D. Kristof and Sheryl WuDunn
A Fine Balance by Rohinton Mistry (fictional, but thematically linked)
